questions.question: How do you parse and generate JSON in Python?
questions.title: Parsing and Generating JSON in Python
questions.direct_answer: Use json.loads() to parse JSON text and json.dumps() to produce JSON text. Use json.load() and json.dump() for file objects. JSON objects become dictionaries, arrays become lists, and malformed input raises JSONDecodeError; decoded data still needs application-level validation.

interviewer_intent.testing: JSON-to-Python type mapping and the load/loads/dump/dumps boundaries.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating JSON as a lossless Python object format or forgetting that parsing does not validate a schema.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention strict-number handling and one type that needs an explicit representation.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: loads() reads a JSON string; load() reads from a file-like object.
dumps() returns a JSON string; dump() writes to a file-like object.
JSON object, array, null, true, and false map to dict, list, None, True, and False.
Encoding or decoding JSON does not validate your business schema.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Python's `json` module converts between JSON text and ordinary Python values. It does not save arbitrary Python objects exactly as they are. Decoding creates new dictionaries, lists, strings, numbers, Booleans, or `None`; encoding chooses JSON text that another language can read.

Use `json.loads(text)` when JSON is already in memory as a string, bytes, or bytearray. Use `json.load(file)` when an open readable file-like object is the source. Both decode one JSON document; the difference is where the input comes from.

Use `json.dumps(value)` when the caller needs a JSON string. Use `json.dump(value, file)` to write JSON text to an open writable file-like object. The encoder returns or writes text, not raw network bytes, so a binary protocol still needs an explicit encoding such as UTF-8.

A JSON object becomes a Python `dict`, an array becomes `list`, strings remain `str`, whole numbers normally become `int`, decimal numbers normally become `float`, and `true`, `false`, and `null` become `True`, `False`, and `None`. Python-only values such as `datetime`, `set`, or a custom class need a documented representation.

Malformed JSON raises `json.JSONDecodeError`, but successful decoding proves only that the text is valid JSON. The result could still be a list when the API promised an object, or contain a string where a number is required. Parse at the boundary, then check the exact fields and types before using the value.

sections.title: The boundary between JSON text and Python values
sections.content:
JSON is a text format, not a Python object store. Serialization chooses a portable representation for a limited set of values; deserialization creates new Python values from that representation. It does not preserve every Python-specific type or object identity.

The s in loads and dumps can be remembered as string. Their counterparts load and dump work with streams. The encoder returns str rather than bytes, so writing JSON to a binary protocol requires an explicit character encoding, normally UTF-8.

Two important boundaries are often missed. First, valid JSON can have a scalar at the top level, so the result is not guaranteed to be a dictionary. Second, Python's default encoder accepts NaN and Infinity even though those names are outside strict JSON; allow_nan=False turns that interoperability issue into a visible ValueError.

After parsing an API payload, validation should describe the actual contract: which keys are required, which may be absent, and what types and ranges are permitted.

sections.title: JSON text and Python values
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  JT[JSON text] -->|loads / load| PV[Python values]
  PV -->|dumps / dump| JT
  PV --> V[Application validation]
  V --> U[Safe use]
```

sections.title: Worked Python example
sections.content:
```python
import json
from io import StringIO

payload = json.loads('{"name": "Ada", "active": true}')
assert payload == {"name": "Ada", "active": True}

text = json.dumps(payload, ensure_ascii=False, allow_nan=False)
assert json.loads(text) == payload

stream = StringIO()
json.dump({"count": 2}, stream)
assert stream.getvalue() == '{"count": 2}'
```

questions.question: When should you use json.load(), json.loads(), json.dump(), and json.dumps()?
questions.title: Choosing the Right Python JSON Function
questions.direct_answer: Choose load or dump when the source or destination is an open file-like object; choose loads or dumps when JSON is already in memory as text or must be returned as text. The functions perform the same core conversion, but their input and output boundaries differ.

interviewer_intent.testing: Choosing the JSON function from the direction of conversion and the input/output boundary.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling json.loads() on a value that response.json() has already decoded.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the stream versus in-memory distinction without memorizing four unrelated functions.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: json.load(file) reads one JSON document from a file-like object.
json.loads(text) parses JSON already held in memory.
json.dump(value, file) writes JSON text to a file-like object.
json.dumps(value) returns JSON text as str.
Do not call json.loads(response.json()); response.json() has already decoded the JSON.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The four JSON functions come from two choices. First choose the direction: `load` functions decode JSON into Python, while `dump` functions encode Python into JSON. Then choose the boundary: the name ending in `s` works with an in-memory string-like value, while the shorter name works with a file-like stream.

Use `json.loads(response_text)` when raw JSON text is already in memory. Use `json.load(config_file)` when the source is an open file or `StringIO`. Both return a Python value. The file form makes the I/O boundary visible and avoids a separate `read()` call when a stream already exists.

Use `json.dumps(settings)` when a function should return JSON text. Use `json.dump(settings, destination)` when it should write that text to a file-like object. `dumps` returns `str`, not `bytes`, and `dump` expects a destination that accepts text.

Requests `response.json()` already returns a Python value. Calling `json.loads(response.json())` tries to decode that dictionary or list as if it were JSON text and usually raises a type error. Either use `response.json()` or decode `response.text`; do not perform both operations on the same body.

Repeatedly calling `json.dump()` into the same file does not automatically create a valid sequence of JSON records. Choose one JSON array or a documented format such as JSON Lines. The example uses all four functions once and shows that each choice changes only the I/O boundary, not the meaning of the decoded value.

Then choose the boundary: the name ending in `s` works with an in-memory string-like value, while the shorter name works with a file-like stream.

sections.title: Choosing the JSON function from the input and output boundary
sections.content:
Think of load and dump as stream operations and loads and dumps as value operations. This makes the call site show where the I/O boundary lives. It also avoids unnecessary read-all or write-all steps when a file object already exists.

The json module is not a framed protocol: repeatedly calling dump() into the same file does not create one valid JSON document. If a system needs a sequence of records, it must choose a real format such as a single JSON array or a documented JSON Lines protocol.

HTTP clients add another layer. A Requests Response can decode its own JSON body; using response.json() is usually clearer than decoding response.text again, while still requiring the same application validation.

sections.title: Match the function to the boundary
sections.content:
| Need | Function | Result |
|---|---|---|
| File/stream → Python | json.load(file) | Python value |
| Text → Python | json.loads(text) | Python value |
| Python → file/stream | json.dump(value, file) | Writes text |
| Python → text | json.dumps(value) | str |

sections.title: Worked Python example
sections.content:
```python
import json
from io import StringIO

source = StringIO('{"limit": 20}')
settings = json.load(source)

text = json.dumps(settings, sort_keys=True)
copy = json.loads(text)

destination = StringIO()
json.dump(copy, destination)
assert json.loads(destination.getvalue()) == {"limit": 20}
```

questions.question: What JSON type and validation mistakes should a Python API client avoid?
questions.title: JSON Type and Validation Pitfalls in Python
questions.direct_answer: A Python API client should not assume that valid JSON has the expected shape or preserves every Python type. It must handle decode errors, check top-level and field types, distinguish missing from null when the contract requires it, and avoid non-standard numeric values in output.

interviewer_intent.testing: JSON grammar, shape validation, and business validation as separate gates.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Collapsing a missing field and a present null value or assuming every valid payload is an object.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use Decimal or allow_nan=False to show where interoperability needs an explicit decision.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Valid JSON may decode to a dict, list, string, number, Boolean, or None.
A missing key and a present key with null are different states.
JSON object keys become strings, so dictionary key types may change.
datetime, Decimal, set, and custom objects need an explicit representation.
Use allow_nan=False when output must be strict JSON.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The decoder checks JSON syntax and performs basic type conversion. It does not prove that the top level is an object, that required fields exist, or that a value satisfies a business rule. A valid payload such as `[1, 2]` is still wrong when the client expects an object with a numeric `price`.

First catch malformed JSON. Next check the expected container and field types. Finally apply business rules such as `price >= 0` or an allowed currency code. Keeping these gates separate produces clearer errors and stops bad data near the API boundary instead of letting it fail later.

`{}` omits `middle_name`, while `{"middle_name": null}` sends the field with a null value. During an update, omission may mean 'leave it unchanged' and null may mean 'clear it'. `data.get("middle_name")` returns `None` for both, so check `"middle_name" in data` when that difference matters.

JSON has no built-in value for `datetime`, `Decimal`, `set`, raw bytes, or an application object. Convert each one to a documented form, such as an ISO 8601 timestamp or a decimal string. JSON object names are strings, and tuples decode as lists, so encoding is not a perfect Python round trip.

For money or other exact decimals, `json.loads(text, parse_float=Decimal)` avoids converting a JSON decimal through binary floating point. When generating JSON for other systems, `allow_nan=False` rejects `NaN` and infinity instead of emitting non-standard tokens. The complete example combines parsing, shape checks, type checks, and a range rule.

sections.title: JSON value shapes and application validation
sections.content:
A useful model has three layers: JSON grammar, data shape, and business meaning. The decoder is responsible only for grammar and basic type conversion. Shape checks decide whether expected containers and fields exist. Business rules decide whether values such as an age, currency code, or state transition are acceptable.

Missing and null need an explicit policy. In a PATCH-like request, omission may mean 'leave unchanged' while null may mean 'clear the value'. Collapsing both to None too early destroys information needed by the update logic.

Numbers also require care. JSON has one number grammar, while Python chooses int or float during normal decoding. Money and other exact decimals may use parse_float=Decimal. When generating strict JSON, allow_nan=False reveals non-finite floats instead of emitting JavaScript-style tokens that another implementation may reject.

sections.title: Three validation gates
Worked Python example
sections.content:
```python
import json
from decimal import Decimal

def parse_price(text: str) -> Decimal:
    data = json.loads(text, parse_float=Decimal)
    if not isinstance(data, dict):
        raise ValueError("expected a JSON object")
    if "price" not in data or not isinstance(data["price"], Decimal):
        raise ValueError("price must be a JSON decimal number")
    if data["price"] < 0:
        raise ValueError("price cannot be negative")
    return data["price"]

assert parse_price('{"price": 19.99}') == Decimal("19.99")
```
